app.title: Exoplanet Radius Explorer
app.summary: A person loads a planet catalogue from a live archive query, a local snapshot or their own CSV, and a banner shows which source is in use. They narrow the sample in a sidebar by detection method, age group, log-scaled radius and period ranges, and quality cuts such as measured values only and maximum relative uncertainty, and headline counts show how much of the catalogue remains. Three tabs then plot the selected sample in two parameter planes and as a one-dimensional projection, with rank correlations, a cluster-bootstrapped comparison of group medians, and bimodality diagnostics recomputed on each change. The selected rows or the full cleaned table can be downloaded as CSV.

task.text: Test whether a trend or a gap in a catalogue population still holds as the sample is restricted by provenance, precision and detection method.

data.text: A public catalogue table with one row per object, holding measured and model-filled physical parameters, their uncertainties, provenance flags and the host each object belongs to.
data.item: a confirmed planet: one catalogue row with its radius, orbital period, host-star age and discovery method

stage.text: exploring and analysing a public catalogue, testing how sample cuts change a population trend

mechanism.text: Sidebar filters build one selection that drives every tab, and the counts, scatter or density plots, correlations, bootstrap table and histogram diagnostics all recompute from it on each change. Each plot can be recoloured or switched between scatter and density, and reference overlays can be turned on and off.

field.text: population statistics on a heterogeneous catalogue in exoplanet astronomy

workflow.name: select a sample from a catalogue and test whether a trend survives stricter cuts

steps.here: Loads in this order: a live archive table query, then a local snapshot, then a synthetic demo file. A CSV uploaded in the sidebar overrides all of them. The table is schema-checked and cleaned, and a banner names the source and warns loudly when the data is synthetic.

steps.step: filter to the items that matter
steps.here: Multiselects for discovery method and stellar age group. Log-uniform range sliders for radius and period. Checkboxes keep or drop rows with no age or period, keep only published radii, and exclude flagged controversial planets. Sliders cap relative age and radius uncertainty, and a field caps distance.

steps.step: track how much of the collection the selection keeps
steps.here: Metrics count the selected planets (with the difference from the full table), how many have an age, a period or a published radius, and how many distinct host stars there are.

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: Log-log scatter or density plots of stellar age against radius and of period against radius. Points can be coloured by provenance, age group, method, insolation or temperature, and hover shows planet and host. Optional overlays add a binned median band, age-group dividers, Earth/Neptune/Jupiter radii, the valley locus and Solar System planets.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Computes the Spearman rank correlation raw, partial with insolation controlled, and per radius provenance. A young-to-old median radius ratio gets a 95% interval from a bootstrap that resamples host stars, for all methods and for transit discoveries only.

steps.step: test for a feature in a one-dimensional projection
steps.here: Within a chosen radius and period window, radius is detrended by period and shown as a histogram, optionally split by provenance. Each subsample gets KDE peak positions, a gap contrast, a Hartigan dip test p-value and a one- versus two-Gaussian BIC difference.
A table shows the selected planets with readable column names. The selection or the full cleaned table can be downloaded as CSV.

distinctive: Each radius is classed as a published measurement or as calculated from mass, and that provenance can colour points, split the statistics or filter out model-derived rows.
Bootstrap intervals resample whole host stars rather than single planets, because planets in one system share a stellar age.
The age-radius correlation is reported both raw and partial with incident flux controlled, so an apparent trend can be checked against a confounder.
Range sliders are uniform in log space because orbital periods span about seven decades.
A diagonal gap is rotated flat by detrending radius with period, then judged by a bin-independent KDE gap contrast next to a dip test and a BIC comparison.
